extracted.intended_audience: Title IX coordinators, school and college administrators, institutional legal counsel, and other recipients of federal education funds responsible for implementing §106.45 grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing grievance processes for allegations of sexual harassment under Title IX, including live hearings, cross-examination, advisor rules, evidence admissibility, decision-maker training, and distinctions between elementary/secondary and postsecondary procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative character and procedural protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX grievance processes retain their character as administrative proceedings in an educational environment, focused on resolving allegations that a respondent committed sex discrimination in the form of sexual harassment against a complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process is different from civil or criminal trials; recipients should structure procedures to produce reliable determinations regarding responsibility while preserving administrative, education-focused aims and procedural protections for both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization for virtual participation in live hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations expressly authorize a recipient, in the recipient's discretion, to allow any or all participants to participate in the live hearing virtually, with technology enabling participants to see and hear each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may conduct the entire live hearing virtually (including witness participation) and should ensure technology permits real-time audio/visual participation; virtual hearings also address concerns such as restraining orders by avoiding in-person proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination must be conducted by a party's advisor and in real time
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-examination at a live hearing must be conducted directly, orally, and in real time by the party's advisor of choice; parties are expressly precluded from conducting cross-examination personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement was added to clarify that submission of written questions (even during a live hearing) does not satisfy §106.45(b)(6)(i). Cross-examination is to occur in real time and be conducted by an advisor, not the party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient obligation to provide an advisor for cross-examination without fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a recipient must provide a party with an advisor to conduct cross-examination at a live hearing, that advisor may be of the recipient's choice, must be provided without fee or charge to the party, and may be, but is not required to be, an attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party lacks an advisor at a hearing, the recipient must provide one aligned with the party's interests (and at no cost). The recipient-provided advisor can be non-attorney and need not be the party's original advisor of choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor status and training do not determine outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's advisor may be, but is not required to be, an attorney, and advisors are not required to be trained; the status or professional qualifications of a party's advisor must not affect the recipient's compliance with §106.45 or the outcome of the grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers are responsible for objectively evaluating all relevant evidence; the Department emphasizes determinations should be based on the merits and evidence rather than the skill or status of an advisor. Recipients should ensure advisor status does not lead to unequal treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and evidence gathering remains on the recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations ensure that the burden of gathering evidence, and the burden of proof, remain on the recipient, not on either party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While parties have procedural rights to participate and to assist from advisors, recipients retain responsibility to investigate and assemble the evidence necessary to reach accurate determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker training and impartiality requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers must be trained to serve impartially and avoid prejudgment of the facts at issue, bias, and conflicts of interest; decision-makers must also be trained in how to determine what questions and evidence are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training for decision-makers should include how to evaluate relevance, assign weight and credibility to evidence in an impartial manner, and avoid sex stereotypes or prejudgment. The regulations do not require training for party advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different procedures for elementary/secondary versus postsecondary institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations preserve §106.45(b)(6)(ii) permitting written questions and optional hearings in elementary and secondary schools, while postsecondary institutions are subject to the live hearing with advisor-conducted cross-examination model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should adapt procedures to students' ages and developmental abilities: written-question models may be appropriate in K–12 contexts, whereas postsecondary students are generally expected to participate in live hearings with advisor-conducted cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of parties during live hearings upon request
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(6)(i) requires recipients to conduct the entire live hearing (not only cross-examination) with the parties located in separate rooms, upon any party's request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects parties who have restraining orders or who prefer not to be in physical proximity. Virtual hearings are a permissible way to maintain separation while enabling participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on admissibility—prior sexual behavior, predisposition, privilege, and treatment records
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions and evidence about a complainant's sexual predisposition are never relevant; questions and evidence about a complainant's prior sexual behavior are not relevant except in two narrow exceptions (to prove someone else committed the alleged misconduct, or where it relates to consent between the complainant and respondent). Information protected by any legally recognized privilege cannot be used. A recipient cannot use a party's treatment records without the party's voluntary, written consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must exclude questions/evidence about predisposition and generally exclude prior sexual behavior except for the two enumerated exceptions. Privileged information and treatment records without consent are barred from use in the grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on excluding relevant evidence by adopting broad evidentiary exclusion rules; weighing relevance impartially
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to impose a comprehensive set of courtroom-style evidentiary rules; decision-makers must consider relevant evidence (inculpatory and exculpatory) and may not adopt rules that exclude relevant evidence for public policy reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although recipients may not exclude relevant evidence categorically (e.g., character evidence) they may evaluate and assign weight or credibility to such evidence impartially. Duplicative evidence may be deemed not relevant. The Department will enforce compliance on relevance but will defer to recipient discretion on weight, absent improper treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliability of unsworn/un-cross-examined statements in postsecondary hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements not subject to cross-examination in postsecondary institutions cannot be relied on by the decision-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers in postsecondary live hearings should not rely on statements for which there was no opportunity for cross-examination; the regulations tie admissibility/reliance to the cross-examination mechanism to protect reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of cross-examination—to equally challenge credibility and reduce erroneous outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-examination is intended to give both parties equal opportunity to meaningfully challenge the plausibility, reliability, credibility, and consistency of the other party and witnesses so that outcomes are more likely to be factually accurate and to reduce erroneous findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-examination is not adopted primarily to protect one side; it is adopted to improve the truth-seeking function of the grievance process and to enhance perceptions of fairness and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator not a party when signing a formal complaint; must remain impartial
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a formal complaint is signed by a Title IX Coordinator, the Title IX Coordinator does not become a party; the Title IX Coordinator must comply with all provisions in §106.45, including the training requirement and the avoidance of bias and conflict of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the Title IX Coordinator testifies as a witness, they are expected to serve impartially. The recipient is not obligated to provide the Title IX Coordinator with an advisor because that obligation attaches only where a party lacks an advisor of choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker authority to ask questions and elicit testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations permit the decision-maker, on the decision-maker's own initiative, to ask questions and elicit testimony from parties and witnesses as part of the recipient's burden to reach a determination regarding responsibility based on objective evaluation of all relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers should actively manage fact-finding by posing questions to clarify testimony and ensure relevant evidence (both inculpatory and exculpatory) is considered in making an objective determination.
